items.text: In contemporary cities, public spaces are increasingly curated as zones  of  consumption  rather  than  participation.  Parks,  plazas, and even sidewalks are redesigned to favor  commercial aesthetics  over  communal  engagement.  Benches  are  replaced with branded kiosks, and open areas become sites for controlled leisure.  This  transformation  signals  not  mere  urban  evolution but a (1) _______ shift in how collectivity is imagined. Citizenship, once  enacted  through  shared  spaces,  is  now  mediated  by transactional encounters.  The  architecture  of  inclusion  has given  way  to the infrastructure of surveillance, where access is contingent on purchase and behavior is continuously monitored. The public realm, in this sense, becomes  an  algorithmic frontier-its openness filtered through predictive analytics. Here, design serves not freedom but compliance, sculpting movement and  interaction  through  invisible boundaries of data. What was once  civic has become (2) _______: a landscape choreographed by capital and coded authority.

items.text: Urban  wilderness,  often  dismissed  as  peripheral  or  accidental, constitutes a lexicon of latent ecologies. Overgrown  lots, cracked  pavements,  and  neglected  waterways  do  not  merely represent neglect; they  inscribe  a  narrative  of  persistence, encoding  resilience  as  (6)  ____.  These  vegetative  anomalies challenge  the  prescriptive  order  of  urban  planning,  proposing instead  an  indeterminate  rhythm  that  is  both  anarchic  and generative.  The  wild,  in  this  framing,  is  not chaos, but a dense articulation of ecological syntax. Its language manifests through tangled  vines  and  fractured  asphalt, resisting the hegemony of manicured parks. To present such wilderness as merely picturesque  is  to engage in epistemic (7)_____-turning survival

TG: @ikunal_x Cloze Test and  resilience  into  superficial  display.  What  is  celebrated  as renewal often entails displacement, where biodiversity is sacrificed  to recreational imaginaries and 'green infrastructure' becomes a euphemism for controlled intervention. To perceive these  spaces  critically is to cultivate (8)_____-an attentiveness to  life  that  thrives  beyond  human  calculation.  These  terrains demand interpretive  patience,  where  fallen  trees  and  seasonal wetlands  become  loci  of  inquiry  and  wonder.  Yet  wilderness defies  containment.  It  is  not  mere  landscape,  but  ontological surplus-a  presence  that  eludes  categorization.  Policy  cannot domesticate  it;  architecture  cannot  tame  it.  It  persists,  liminal and  instructive,  as  a  (9)_____grammar  inscribed  upon  urban peripheries. The city's wilds are not neglected. They are semiotic punctuations-interruptions  in  the  metropolitan  narrative  that insist  on  recognition  not  as  absence,  but  as  ecological  (10)
_____.
